properties.name: VERIFIES cannot target an Interface, so no contract in any reflow2 design can carry a check — and interfaces are the nodes MOSA turns on
properties.statement:
FOUND 2026-08-21 while fixing the finding "nothing verifies ifc:core-api". The fix was refused by the edge validator:

  Invalid edge: VERIFIES cannot connect Verification to Interface

The schema enumerates VERIFIES targets as **Capability, Requirement, Artifact, Component, DesignRule, Constraint**. Interface is absent.

SO REFLOW2 CAN ATTACH EVIDENCE TO A RULE, A BUDGET, A PART, A FILE, A CAPABILITY AND A REQUIREMENT — AND NOT TO A CONTRACT. Every Interface in every design using reflow2 is unverifiable by construction. reflow2's own 17 interfaces have zero incoming VERIFIES edges, and that reads as "nobody wrote one" when the truth is "nobody could".

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A MISSING EDGE TYPE USUALLY WOULD. A contract is the node a modular open-systems approach turns on — `set_interface_designation`'s own description calls `published` "the distinction a systems-engineering ICD publishes and that MOSA calls a modular system interface". The question "does this boundary actually hold?" is the most natural thing anyone would want to check about a published contract, and it is the one question this vocabulary cannot express. `ifc:mcp-tools` is specified 9 of 9 fields, is the surface every user's agent calls, and cannot carry a single piece of evidence that it behaves as specified.

⭐ IT MAY BE THE THIRD INSTANCE OF A PATTERN THIS EDGE HAS ALREADY RECORDED ABOUT ITSELF. `schema/verify.yaml` carries a long comment on VERIFIES under-enumerating its targets twice: the extraction hint named three types while four were true, and later the `to` list itself was derived from a census that found five types by edge count and MISSED TWO carrying one edge each — which made an existing export unimportable by the binary that wrote it for four days while every gate read green. Its own words: "a schema tightening that silently orphans existing data is a breaking change wearing a validation error's clothes." Interface may simply be the next unlisted-but-wanted target, never censused because no edge existed to count — an absence cannot appear in a survey of what is present.

WHAT THIS FACT DOES NOT SETTLE: whether Interface SHOULD be added. That is a schema change and Anthony's call. Two things argue for care rather than speed — the same comment warns that narrowing this list broke a real design, so widening it deserves the same scrutiny in reverse; and it is worth asking first what a check on a contract would MEAN, since a conformance test against a specified boundary is a different kind of evidence from a unit test on a capability.

NOTE ON THE STAMP: the schema stamp carries node and edge TYPE NAMES, not their target lists, so adding Interface to this `to` list would not move it and would owe no upgrade note.
